newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stocks seen steady, focus on Telecom.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks seen steady, focus on Telecom.

text.p: The outlook for Hong Kong stocks in the coming week looks mixed, with strong forces pulling sentiment in opposite directions, but brokers are generally upbeat.
"I think the market will probably move sideways next week after such strong gains (of the past month)," said Peter So, deputy head of research at Schroders Securities.
"And it might edge up a bit. Market sentiment is still good and the underlying tone is still very firm."
The Hang Seng Index closed 140.39 points lower at 14,655.13 on Friday after a volatile session which saw the index moving in a 366-point range.
Over the week, the index shed 102.68 points or 0.70 percent.

Before the minor correction last week, the index had risen more than 2,500 points in less than two months, fuelled by buying from both institutional and retail investors seeking exposure to the positive aspects of Hong Kong's handover to Chinese sovereignty on July 1.
Turnover set a single-day record of HK$26.48 billion last Monday.
The stock exchange will be closed on Monday to mark a local holiday. Normal trading will resume on Tuesday.
Boosting sentiment in the coming week will be the U.S. stock and bond markets' positive reaction to the May employment report, brokers said.

The Dow Jones Industrials closed 130.49 points higher at 7,435.78 following the release of the report on Friday, and the U.S. long bond closed up 1-8/32 at 98-1/32 to yield 6.78 percent, its lowest yield since February 28.
The report showed a fall in the May unemployment rate to 4.8 percent, the lowest rate since October 1973.

But other data, in particular a moderate level of wage increases during the month, pointed to continued strong, steady growth in the U.S. economy with limited upward pressure on prices, U.S. economists said.

The announcement by Cable & Wireless Plc on Friday that it was selling a 5.5 percent stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd to the Chinese Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications should have a strong, positive impact on market sentiment, brokers said.
But they also cautioned that any near- to medium-term benefit of the Chinese investment may already be reflected in Telecom's price.

Hong Kong Telecom, which set a record close on Friday of HK$19.00, has risen HK$4.00, or nearly 27 percent since May 9 when CITIC Pacific Ltd announced it was selling its 7.74 percent holding to China Everbright Holdings Co Ltd.
"Telecom rose HK$1.90 (on Friday). Without that, the index would have been down another 150 points or so," said a broker at BZW Securities.

Brokers said a directive from the People's Bank of China that would ban state banks from trading on China's stock markets could have a knock-on effect in Hong Kong and take some of the fire out of red chips and other "China concept" stocks.

"Red chips have already come off," said the BZW broker. "It is too early to tell what the impact of this measure will be, but I think the market should correct a little bit further. It is long overdue."
Brokers also warned the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was again talking about putting guidelines on banks' mortgage lending.
"Property shares led the market down (on Friday) and people are worried about the government measures," said Allen Pao in institutional sales at South China Securities.
The property subindex dropped 3.25 percent to 25,312.71 compared with the index's 0.95 percent fall.
